subject: predatory katydid
title: This Insect Answers a Cicada's Love Song. Then It Eats the Singer

scenes.text: A male cicada sings. The wrong female answers.
In the Australian outback, a female cicada answers a male's song with a quick flick of her wings. That click means: come closer.
The spotted predatory katydid has learned to make that click, at exactly the right moment.
It even jerks its body like a female would.
The male walks straight into its reach, and gets eaten.
It works on cicada species it has never even met. The song gets answered, just not by a cicada.

description:
A male cicada sings to find a mate, and in arid inland Australia the reply sometimes comes from a predator.
The spotted predatory katydid, Chlorobalius leucoviridis, imitates the wing-flick reply of a receptive female cicada with clicks of its own wings and matching jerks of its body, luring the male within reach. In experiments it could do this for the songs of many cicada species, including ones it had never encountered (Marshall and Hill, PLoS ONE, 2009).
Would you have fallen for it? Comment below.
first_comment: Biologists call this aggressive mimicry: the predator copies something its prey wants. Which other animal lies to get dinner?
